Blood of the Covenant
BLUD uv thuh KUV-uh-nunt
noun phrase / doctrine
Blood (Old English blod, the vital fluid; in biblical usage, the carrier of life, Lev 17:11) + of the covenant (from Old French covenant, agreement, treaty, from Latin convenire). The phrase “blood of the covenant” translates Hebrew dam haberit (Exod 24:8; Zech 9:11) and Greek haima tēs diathēkēs (Matt 26:28; Heb 9:20). In biblical covenantal theology, covenants are ratified by blood: the slaughter of animals and the application of their blood to the covenant parties (the covenant-cutting ritual of Gen 15) or to the covenant community (the Sinai blood-sprinkling of Exod 24) seals the covenant's binding force. Blood ratification thus signifies both life-oath (“may I die like this animal if I break this covenant”) and life-gift (the life of the sacrifice poured out in the covenant's inauguration).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The blood of the covenant is the atoning, ratifying blood that seals the binding relationship between God and His people — in type, the blood of sacrificial animals at Sinai (Exod 24:8); in antitype and fulfillment, the blood of Jesus Christ poured out at Calvary for the ratification of the new covenant (Matt 26:28; Heb 9:20). Exodus 24:8 records the Sinai ratification: Moses took the blood of young bulls sacrificed as burnt offerings and peace offerings, “sprinkled it on the people, and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant which the LORD has made with you according to all these words.'” The blood was first sprinkled on the altar (representing God's side) and then on the people — a bilateral act of covenant-sealing that bound both parties to the covenant's terms. Hebrews 9:20 quotes Exodus 24:8 in its discussion of the superiority of Christ's priestly work, establishing the typological lineage: the Sinai blood pointed forward to a better blood. Zechariah 9:11 announces the covenant-blood as the ground of liberation: “As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit.” The new covenant's blood is Christ's own blood: Matthew 26:28 records His words of institution at the Last Supper, “For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins.” Hebrews 13:20 calls Christ's blood “the blood of the eternal covenant,” establishing its permanent, unrepeatable, eternally valid character. The blood of the covenant is the ground of every covenant benefit: justification, forgiveness, adoption, sanctification, and final glorification all rest on this poured-out blood.

Webster 1828 Definition

The blood of the covenant is the atoning, ratifying blood that seals God's covenant with His people — in type, the Sinai blood-sprinkling of Exodus 24:8; in fulfillment, the blood of Jesus Christ poured out for the forgiveness of sins (Matt 26:28) and the ratification of the new covenant.

BLOOD OF THE COVENANT. Hebrew dam haberit; Greek haima tēs diathēkēs: the blood by which a covenant is ratified and sealed, applied to the covenant parties as the binding oath-sacrifice that inaugurates the covenant relationship.

2. Sinai ratification (Exod 24:3–8): Moses reads the Book of the Covenant; the people confess covenant allegiance; animals are sacrificed; blood is divided — half sprinkled on the altar (God's side) and half sprinkled on the people (Israel's side); Moses declares “this is the blood of the covenant.” The covenant is doubly ratified by blood touching both parties.

3. Covenantal blood-ratification theology: in the ancient Near Eastern treaty pattern (and in the Abrahamic covenant of Gen 15), animals are slaughtered and the parties pass between them, invoking the oath: “may I become like these animals if I break this covenant.” At Sinai, God graciously binds Himself with Israel through blood rather than requiring Israel alone to pass between the pieces.

4. Christ's words of institution (Matt 26:28): “this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins” — the Sinai formula echoed and surpassed; the better blood of the better covenant (Heb 9:23; 12:24) ratifying the eternal covenant between God and His elect in Christ.

5. The blood's covenant-benefits: Hebrews 13:20–21 prays through “the blood of the eternal covenant” for sanctification; Zechariah 9:11 grounds liberation from captivity in the covenant-blood; Revelation 12:11 describes the overcomers conquering “by the blood of the Lamb.” Every covenant benefit flows from the poured-out blood.

Key Scripture

Exod 24:8 — "And Moses took the blood, sprinkled it on the people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant which the LORD has made with you according to all these words.”"

Heb 9:20 — "saying, “This is the blood of the covenant which God commanded you.”"

Matt 26:28 — "For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins."

Zech 9:11 — "As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit."

Modern Corruption

The blood of the covenant has been thinned by liberal theology's substitution of moral influence for penal substitution (no blood-curse; only love exemplified) and by modern evangelical squeamishness about blood-language in worship, which strips away the covenant-sealing weight that Scripture consistently attaches to the shedding of blood for the ratification of covenant.

expand to see more

Liberal Protestant theology from Schleiermacher through modern progressive evangelicalism has systematically replaced the blood-covenant framework with a moral-influence model: Christ's death demonstrates God's love; no actual legal curse is borne; no wrath is propitiated; no covenant-sealing blood is required. This trajectory ends in a theology where “blood” language in hymns and liturgy is revised as primitive or offensive (“Are You Washed in the Blood?” excised from hymnals; “the blood of Jesus” replaced with “the self-giving of Jesus”). The dictionary holds that the blood-language of Scripture is not dispensable metaphor but covenant-essential description: Hebrews 9:22 states it plainly: “without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” The new covenant is a blood covenant; remove the blood and you remove the covenant.

The broader evangelical squeamishness about blood imagery reflects a therapeutic-culture aversion to sacrifice, death, and curse-bearing as primary categories. Worship teams edit out the blood from contemporary songs; preachers avoid the language of wrath and propitiation in favor of therapeutic relational categories. The 1689 LBCF's description of Christ as having “offered himself a sacrifice” and purchased the church “with his own blood” (8.5) is not merely a doctrinal statement about soteriology; it is the covenant-ratification language that grounds every benefit the elect receive. Sanitizing it is not cultural wisdom; it is covenant-content removal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The blood of the covenant roots in the creation-order connection between blood and life (Lev 17:11), in the Abrahamic covenant's animal-cutting ratification (Gen 15), in the Sinai blood-sprinkling that inaugurated the Mosaic covenant (Exod 24), and in Christ's poured-out blood as the definitive, eternal covenant-ratifying sacrifice (Heb 9:12–14; 13:20).

expand to see more

Leviticus 17:11 — blood and life: “the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood by reason of the life that makes atonement”; the life of the sacrifice offered in place of the forfeited life of the sinner

Genesis 15 — the Abrahamic blood-covenant: God passes between the animal pieces (as a smoking fire pot and flaming torch) while Abram sleeps, taking the full covenant oath upon Himself; the blood ratification is unilateral on God's side, grounding the covenant's unconditional character

Exodus 24:3–8 — Sinai blood-sprinkling: the blood divided between altar and people; Moses' declaration “this is the blood of the covenant”; the entire Mosaic covenant system inaugurated by blood, sustained by blood sacrifice, and pointing forward to the better blood

Matthew 26:28 — Christ's words of institution: “my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins”; the Sinai formula echoed and completed; the better covenant (Heb 7:22) ratified by a better blood (Heb 12:24)

Hebrews 9:12–14; 13:20 — eternal covenant blood: Christ's blood obtains eternal redemption (not annual reprieve); it is the blood of the eternal covenant; it cleanses the conscience from dead works; all blessing flows from this poured-out life

Usage

"Hebrews 9:22 — “without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” — is the most compact statement of the blood-covenant principle in the New Testament. It explains why the entire Levitical sacrificial system was blood-centered (not culture, not aesthetics), and why Christ's atoning work had to be the shedding of blood. The forgiveness the new covenant delivers is not an administrative decision; it is a covenant-sealing event requiring the pouring out of covenant-blood."

"Zechariah 9:11's announcement — “because of the blood of your covenant, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit” — applies the covenant-blood directly to liberation from captivity. The blood of the covenant is not merely forgiveness-theology; it is the ground of every redemptive act, including the final resurrection and liberation of those who have died in faith. The eschatological hope of the redeemed is blood-purchased."

"The Lord's Supper cup (the cup of blessing, 1 Cor 10:16; Luke 22:20) is the regular covenant-renewal instrument through which the blood of the covenant is proclaimed until Christ comes. Every Supper announces the same covenant-ratifying blood that Moses sprinkled at Sinai, now applied to the conscience by the Spirit through faith — the eternal covenant renewed in the cup at every gathering of the covenant people."
